decisions.mechanismComparison: Herald and the original change-lifecycle cluster govern verified release communication but not technical-channel syndication. Chorus already owns claim-provenance editorial briefs, channel-native derivatives, repurposing, and measured editorial review without account action; Beacon adds discoverability, indexing, channel sequencing, and validated growth analysis. The certified Wave 2 editorial package confirms that bounded channel adaptation remains under Chorus rather than publication ownership.
decisions.rationale: Retain canonical URL, tag, and destination-format details as supporting patterns for the existing Chorus and Beacon composition. They add no independent authority, terminal artifact, or reason to create a release-owned syndication skill.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Herald can design release gates and Daedalus can govern test-first local engineering, but neither contract binds Bash dialect, strict-mode edge cases, quoted and resolved paths, error traps, privilege and destructive-action controls, Bats fixture isolation, stream assertions, and filesystem side-effect proof into one operational contract.
decisions.rationale: Preserve the combined Bash and Bats mechanism as a focused operational skill beneath Herald and Daedalus. It is too narrow for a Godskill and must not inherit deployment, privilege, or destructive authority.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Daedalus already owns evidence-led local refactoring, dependency and configuration inspection, bounded removal, test-first verification, rollback, and specialist handoff. Herald contributes readiness boundaries but does not own the source edits; Lovable and Radix names are project-specific evidence rather than a new capability.
decisions.rationale: Keep the cleanup sequence as a Daedalus refactoring pattern and let Herald consume its verified build result. A separate exported-app cleanup owner would duplicate implementation authority around one generator ecosystem.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Daedalus owns compatibility, rollback, local migration, test-first change, and framework boundaries, while Herald owns downstream readiness. Neither current contract explicitly requires dependency-why mapping, semver and peer ordering, lockfile baselines, one-major-at-a-time advancement, selective generator merges, or one-by-one framework-default activation.
decisions.rationale: Extend Daedalus's migration route with the missing dependency and framework-upgrade specialization, then hand its verified result to Herald. This preserves one implementation owner and keeps staging or publication authority separate.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Herald can specify quality gates and Phoenix can analyze supplied baselines, workloads, metrics, and regressions read-only. Neither owns authorized load generation across HTTP, browser, and WebSocket targets, shared test data, tagged thresholds, custom metrics, target cleanup, or retaining machine-readable artifacts when the CI gate fails.
decisions.rationale: Create one focused operational skill with explicit target ownership, load budget, data-mutation, cleanup, and third-party authority gates. Its evidence feeds Herald and Phoenix, but their current effect contracts must not be widened to run external load.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Herald's delivery route owns repository stack discovery, quality gates, environments, and failure feedback, and Daedalus owns local configuration edits. The current contracts do not bind package-owned tasks, workspace dependency ordering, cache input and output declarations, environment hash coverage, affected selection, overrides, and transit-node invalidation.
decisions.rationale: Extend Herald's continuous-delivery design with a monorepo graph and cache-correctness specialization while delegating implementation changes to Daedalus and preserving registry publication as a separate effect.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Herald already governs version boundaries, delivery gates, dependency-name screening, and release-unit closure, while the legacy Python cluster correctly keeps registry publication ecosystem-specific. Herald does not yet require pnpm workspace topology, content-addressed strict resolution, catalogs, overrides and patches, peer policy, frozen CI, install-script approval, or SBOM evidence.
decisions.rationale: Extend Herald with the local reproducibility and package-handoff contract, not registry execution. Exact package-manager commands, credentials, installation, and publication remain current ecosystem adapters or human-owned effects.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Herald and the original production-readiness cluster can consume local installability, health, and rollback evidence but do not own the implementation. Daedalus owns named-platform implementation, runtime compatibility, test-first local change, and rollback, but its language-framework route does not state manifest and icon acceptance, service-worker install and activate transitions, versioned cache cleanup, request-class fetch strategies, offline fallbacks, or Lighthouse and device proof. The certified browser-game cluster covers browser lifecycle and offline packaging choices for games, not installable PWA cache semantics.
decisions.rationale: Add a PWA specialization to Daedalus rather than creating a release publisher. Hosting, push, sync conflict, and production service-worker rollout remain explicit handoffs.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Aegis already owns agent and MCP permission audits, command boundaries, dependency trust, least privilege, separation of duties, evidence-ranked mitigation, rollback or revocation, and authority decisions. Herald has no permission-grant route and delegates unresolved authority; repository marker and package-manager detection are narrower implementation patterns.
decisions.rationale: Keep the concrete read-only settings heuristic as evidence for Aegis and do not create release-agent permission ownership under Herald. Provider-specific settings and wildcard semantics still require current review.

decisions.mechanismComparison: Logos already owns provenance-bearing documentation planning, drafting, updating, maintenance context, technical explanation, structural extraction, source boundaries, uncertainty, and publication refusal. Herald supplies verified release facts but does not own README prose; repository and deployment-marker inspection are evidence inputs to Logos rather than a distinct owner.
decisions.rationale: Route repository-derived README construction to Logos with Herald as a release-evidence source. Preserve the reviewed section and troubleshooting patterns without duplicating documentation authority.
